title: composition and occasion
short: Composed near Leghorn (Livorno) in summer 1820 after an evening walk; published with Prometheus Unbound (1820).
body: Mary Shelley's note on the poems of 1820 records that the poem was inspired while 'wandering among the lanes whose myrtle-hedges were the bowers of the fire-flies' near Leghorn, when they heard a skylark singing. The skylark (Alauda arvensis) sings while rising high into the sky, often until it is invisible, which gives the poem its controlling idea of a voice heard but not seen. 'Hail to thee' is a formula of greeting to a superior being, as in the angel's 'Hail' to Mary (Luke 1:28); 'blithe' means joyful, light-hearted.

title: Bird thou never wert
short: The poet denies the lark is a bird at all: it is a spirit; the line is a provocative refusal of natural description.
body: Critics have long debated the line. Some take it literally as Platonist: the song comes from a higher realm and the bird is only its vehicle. Others take it as hyperbole, a way of saying the singer's art transcends its nature. Wordsworth's skylark poems keep the bird bound to its nest; Shelley's goes the other way. 'Wert' is an archaic second-person past form of 'be'.

title: unpremeditated art
short: Art that is spontaneous, without forethought; Shelley echoes Milton's claim that his muse inspires his "unpremeditated Verse".
body: In Paradise Lost 9.24 Milton describes his heavenly muse dictating to him in sleep, inspiring 'Easy my unpremeditated verse'. Shelley borrows the phrase for the bird, making it the model of the inspired poet. The idea fits the Defence of Poetry, which insists that poetry is not produced by labour and study but comes from inspiration. The paradox of 'art' that is unpremeditated (art usually implying skill and design) is the stanza's point.

title: the stanza
short: Twenty-one five-line stanzas: four short trochaic lines and a long final alexandrine (iambic hexameter), rhymed ababb.
body: The short lines, three stresses each, rising and quick, mimic the lark's darting ascent; the final long line spreads out like the song lingering in the air. The contrast between brevity and expansiveness gives each stanza a rise and release. The rhyme scheme ababb lets the last line echo the fourth. The poem moves from address (st. 1-6), through a series of similes (st. 7-12), to questions and reflections on human limits (st. 13-21).

title: cloud of fire
short: The rising bird is likened to a fiery cloud, with an echo of the pillar of fire and cloud that guided Israel (Exodus 13:21).
body: In Exodus the Lord goes before the Israelites 'by day in a pillar of a cloud' and 'by night in a pillar of fire'. Shelley fuses the two in one image of light and lift. The comparison is the first of many that try and fail to say what the bird is: the poem's method is to multiply similes because no single one is adequate.

title: an unbodied joy
short: A joy without a body: pure emotion, free of the physical; the lark is felt as feeling itself.
body: The adjective was a favourite of Shelley's: abstractions without bodies recur in his work. The line suggests the ideal of a spirit freed from mortality. 'Whose race is just begun' adds the image of a runner starting a race, connected to Psalm 19:5, where the sun 'rejoiceth as a strong man to run a race'. The sunset setting (st. 3-4) means the lark flies in the last light, so its joy contrasts with the falling day.

title: even
short: Evening (poetic contraction); the colours of dusk "melt" around the bird.
body: 'Even' for evening is archaic and poetic. The stanza describes the lark invisible in the evening light, 'Like a star of Heaven, / In the broad daylight': a star is present in daytime but cannot be seen. The lark too is heard but not seen. The paradox of invisible presence governs the next stanzas. The colour words (pale, purple) also mark the poem's fascination with fading, half-visible light.

title: that silver sphere
short: Probably the morning star (Venus) fading at dawn; some readers take it as the moon. Either way it is felt rather than seen.
body: The 'silver sphere' whose 'intense lamp narrows / In the white dawn clear' is usually identified as Venus as the morning star, which is the last star visible as day breaks. Some commentators suggest the moon, but the moon is mentioned separately in the next stanza, which favours Venus. 'Keen as are the arrows' links the planet to Artemis/Diana, goddess of the moon and an archer, which may be why some readers prefer the moon. The point is the paradox in 'we hardly see—we feel that it is there'.

anchor: What thou art we know not
title: What thou art we know not
short: The turning point of the poem: after trying to describe the bird directly, the poet admits ignorance and begins a series of similes.
body: The admission prepares four long similes (st. 8-11), each introduced by 'Like': a poet, a high-born maiden, a glow-worm, a rose. Each presents something hidden that yet communicates itself (through song, music, light, scent). The method has been called the poem's characteristic Shelleyan 'failure' of definition: the lark's essence can be approached only through comparisons that never quite reach it.

title: the Poet hidden in light
short: The lark is like a poet hidden "In the light of thought", whose songs move the world to sympathy with unnoticed hopes and fears.
body: This is the first and most important simile, because it states Shelley's theory of the poet. The poet is invisible, his influence unacknowledged, but his songs make the world 'wrought / To sympathy'. The Defence of Poetry compares the poet to 'a nightingale, who sits in darkness and sings to cheer its own solitude', whose listeners are moved without knowing why. 'Wrought' means worked, brought to a state.

sources.cite: P. B. Shelley, A Defence of Poetry (written 1821, publ. 1840)

title: high-born maiden
short: A romance image: a lady in a tower sings in secret to ease her love, and her music overflows her chamber.
body: The maiden in a tower is a stock figure of medieval romance and its Gothic revivals. Her song, like the lark's, is unseen but escapes its confinement. 'Bower' in older usage meant a lady's private chamber. The 'secret hour' and 'love-laden soul' introduce desire, which the poem will later contrast with the lark's love without 'sad satiety'. The image makes the lark's song an expression of private feeling that becomes public by overflow.

title: glow-worm
short: The glow-worm's light, hidden among grass and flowers, scatters unseen; "aereal" means airy, of the air.
body: The glow-worm (in fact a beetle) shines in the dark. Mary Shelley's note on the Leghorn summer mentions the fireflies flashing in the myrtle hedges, so the image may come from the walk that inspired the poem. 'Aereal hue' (the archive keeps the older spelling) means an airy or ethereal colour. 'Unbeholden' means unseen, though it can also suggest 'not indebted'.

title: the rose and the bees
short: A rose hidden in its leaves, its scent "deflowered" by winds, overpowers the bees ("heavy-winged thieves") with too much sweetness.
body: The simile is sensual and slightly disquieting: 'deflowered' and 'thieves' suggest violation, and 'faint with too much sweet' an excess that becomes pain. Critics have noted that this stanza anticipates the poem's later theme of joy mixed with suffering ('Our sweetest songs are those that tell of saddest thought'). The bees, laden with pollen, are 'heavy-winged', in contrast to the light-winged lark.

title: Sprite or Bird
short: "Sprite" is a spirit or fairy; the poet now leaves the question of the lark's nature open.
body: After declaring 'Bird thou never wert' (st. 1), the poet now allows both possibilities. The shift marks the poem's movement from rapture to questioning: from st. 13 onwards the poet asks the lark to 'teach' him the source of its joy. 'Sprite' is a doublet of 'spirit' (both from Latin spiritus). The request 'Teach us' frames the bird as a teacher and the poet as a pupil, a reversal of the usual relation between poet and subject.

title: Chorus Hymeneal
short: A wedding song, named from Hymen, the Greek god of marriage; with "triumphal chant", the two great public forms of joyful song.
body: Classical weddings were celebrated with a hymenaios, a song invoking Hymen. Triumphal chants were sung for victorious generals in Rome. Shelley says that these human festive forms, compared with the lark's song, are 'but an empty vaunt' (a hollow boast), lacking something essential. 'Want' means lack. The two forms together stand for the highest occasions of shared human joy, love and victory, and both are found wanting beside the solitary bird.

title: satiety
short: Satiety is the weariness that comes after a desire is satisfied; the lark loves without the disillusion that follows human love.
body: The idea that fulfilment kills desire is a commonplace from Lucretius onwards, and Shelley treats it often. 'Joyance' (st. 16) is an archaic word for joy, used by Spenser; 'languor' is the listlessness that follows passion. The lark knows love without that after-sadness, which makes it a figure of an ideal state unavailable to humans. The stanza thus prepares the turn to human limitation in the stanzas that follow.

title: We look before and after
short: An echo of Hamlet: man, made with "such large discourse, / Looking before and after", is a creature of memory and anticipation.
body: In the soliloquy 'How all occasions do inform against me' (Hamlet 4.4, found only in the Second Quarto), Hamlet says God gave humans reason, 'Looking before and after', that should not rust unused. Shelley turns the capacity into a curse: because we look before and after, we 'pine for what is not'. The lark lives in the present; humans, conscious of past and future, cannot. This stanza is the emotional centre of the poem.

title: Our sweetest songs
short: The most famous line of the poem: human art is most beautiful when it expresses sorrow.
body: The line names a Romantic paradox: the lark's song is pure joy, but human beauty depends on pain. The stanza's progression ('sincerest laughter / With some pain is fraught') leads to it. The next stanza adds that even if we were free of hate, pride and fear, we could not reach the lark's joy. The line echoes widely in later poetry; Keats's 'Ode on Melancholy' (1819) makes a related claim that melancholy dwells with beauty.

title: the closing prayer
short: The poem ends with a plea: if the poet had half the lark's joy, the world would listen to him as he listens to the bird.
body: 'Harmonious madness' recalls the Platonic idea of the poet's divine madness (Plato, Phaedrus 245a; Ion), in which inspiration overcomes reason. The final line turns from bird to audience: 'The world should listen then—as I am listening now.' The poet's ambition is for influence, a concern of all Shelley's later writing. The lark is 'scorner of the ground', a final epithet that sums up its freedom.
